L199: 
L200: A percent-encode set is a cite109†set†infra.spec.whatwg.org of cite91†code points†infra.spec.whatwg.org .
L201: 
L202: The C0 control percent-encode set is a cite110†percent-encode set consisting of cite111†C0 controls†infra.spec.whatwg.org and all cite91†code points†infra.spec.whatwg.org greater than U+007E (~).
L203: The fragment percent-encode set is a cite110†percent-encode set consisting of the cite112†C0 control percent-encode set and U+0020 SPACE, U+0022 ("), U+003C (<), U+003E (>), and U+0060 (`).
L204: 
L205: The query percent-encode set is a cite110†percent-encode set consisting of the cite112†C0 control percent-encode set and U+0020 SPACE, U+0022 ("), U+0023 (#), U+003C (<), and U+003E (>).
L206: 
L207: The cite113†query percent-encode set cannot be defined in terms of the cite114†fragment percent-encode set due to the omission of U+0060 (`).
L208: The special-query percent-encode set is a cite110†percent-encode set consisting of the cite113†query percent-encode set and U+0027 (').
L209: 
L210: The path percent-encode set is a cite110†percent-encode set consisting of the cite113†query percent-encode set and U+003F (?), U+005E (^), U+0060 (`), U+007B ({), and U+007D (}).
L211: The userinfo percent-encode set is a cite110†percent-encode set consisting of the cite115†path percent-encode set and U+002F (/), U+003A (:), U+003B (;), U+003D (=), U+0040 (@), U+005B ([) to U+005D (]), inclusive, and U+007C (|).
L212: 
L213: The component percent-encode set is a cite110†percent-encode set consisting of the cite116†userinfo percent-encode set and U+0024 ($) to U+0026 (&), inclusive, U+002B (+), and U+002C (,).
L214: This is used by HTML for `cite117†registerProtocolHandler()†html.spec.whatwg.org `, and could also be used by other standards to percent-encode data that can then be embedded in a cite118†URL ’s cite119†path , cite120†query , or cite121†fragment ; or in an cite73†opaque host . Using it with cite122†UTF-8 percent-encode gives identical results to JavaScript’s cite123†`encodeURIComponent()` [sic]†tc39.es . cite63†[HTML] cite124†[ECMA-262] L215: The `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` percent-encode set is a cite110†percent-encode set consisting of the cite125†component percent-encode set and U+0021 (!), U+0027 (') to U+0029 RIGHT PARENTHESIS, inclusive, and U+007E (~).
L216: 
L217: The cite126†`application/x-www-form-urlencoded` percent-encode set contains all code points, except the cite127†ASCII alphanumeric†infra.spec.whatwg.org , U+002A (*), U+002D (-), U+002E (.), and U+005F (_).
L218: To percent-encode after encoding, given an cite128†encoding†encoding.spec.whatwg.org `encoding`, cite106†scalar value string†infra.spec.whatwg.org `input`, and a cite110†percent-encode set `percentEncodeSet`:
L219: 
L220:   1. cite129†Assert†infra.spec.whatwg.org : `encoding` is cite130†UTF-8†encoding.spec.whatwg.org or `percentEncodeSet` is cite131†special-query percent-encode set or cite126†`application/x-www-form-urlencoded` percent-encode set .
L221:   2. Let `spaceAsPlus` be true if `percentEncodeSet` is cite126†`application/x-www-form-urlencoded` percent-encode set ; otherwise false.
L222: 
L223:   3. Let `encoder` be the result of cite132†getting an encoder†encoding.spec.whatwg.org from `encoding`.
L224: 
L225:   4. Let `inputQueue` be `input` converted to an cite133†I/O queue†encoding.spec.whatwg.org .
L226: 
L227:   5. Let `output` be the empty string.
L228: 
L229:   6. Let `potentialError` be 0.
L230: 
L231: This needs to be a non-null value to initiate the subsequent while loop.
L232:   7. While `potentialError` is non-null:
L233: 
L234:     1. Let `encodeOutput` be an empty cite133†I/O queue†encoding.spec.whatwg.org .
L235: 
L236:     2. Set `potentialError` to the result of running cite134†encode or fail†encoding.spec.whatwg.org with `inputQueue`, `encoder`, and `encodeOutput`.
L237: 
L238:     3. For each `byte` of `encodeOutput` converted to a byte sequence:
L239: 
L240:       1. If `spaceAsPlus` is true and `byte` is 0x20 (SP), then append U+002B (+) to `output` and cite135†continue†infra.spec.whatwg.org .
L241:       2. Let `isomorph` be a cite91†code point†infra.spec.whatwg.org whose cite136†value†infra.spec.whatwg.org is `byte`’s cite137†value†infra.spec.whatwg.org .
L242: 
L243:       3. Assert: `percentEncodeSet` includes all non-cite138†ASCII code points†infra.spec.whatwg.org .
L244: 
L245:       4. If `isomorph` is not in `percentEncodeSet`, then append `isomorph` to `output`.
L246: 
L247:       5. Otherwise, cite139†percent-encode `byte` and append the result to `output`.
L248:     4. If `potentialError` is non-null, then append "`%26%23`", followed by the shortest sequence of cite80†ASCII digits†infra.spec.whatwg.org representing `potentialError` in base ten, followed by "`%3B`", to `output`.
L249: 
L250: This can happen when `encoding` is not cite130†UTF-8†encoding.spec.whatwg.org .
L251: 
L252:   8. Return `output`.
L253: Of the possible values for the `percentEncodeSet` argument only two end up encoding U+0025 (%) and thus give “roundtripable data”: cite125†component percent-encode set and cite126†`application/x-www-form-urlencoded` percent-encode set . The other values for the `percentEncodeSet` argument — which happen to be used by the cite140†URL parser — leave U+0025 (%) untouched and as such it needs to be cite141†percent-encoded first in order to be properly represented.
L254: To UTF-8 percent-encode a cite142†scalar value†infra.spec.whatwg.org `scalarValue` using a `percentEncodeSet`, return the result of running cite143†percent-encode after encoding with cite130†UTF-8†encoding.spec.whatwg.org , `scalarValue` as a cite90†string†infra.spec.whatwg.org , and `percentEncodeSet`.
L255: To UTF-8 percent-encode a cite106†scalar value string†infra.spec.whatwg.org `input` using a `percentEncodeSet`, return the result of running cite143†percent-encode after encoding with cite130†UTF-8†encoding.spec.whatwg.org , `input`, and `percentEncodeSet`.

L274: ## 2. Security considerations
L275: 
L276: The security of a cite118†URL is a function of its environment. Care is to be taken when rendering, interpreting, and passing cite118†URLs around.
L277: When rendering and allocating new cite118†URLs "spoofing" needs to be considered. An attack whereby one cite71†host or cite118†URL can be confused for another. For instance, consider how 1/l/I, m/rn/rri, 0/O, and а/a can all appear eerily similar. Or worse, consider how U+202A LEFT-TO-RIGHT EMBEDDING and similar cite91†code points†infra.spec.whatwg.org are invisible. cite146†[UTR36] L278: When passing a cite118†URL from party `A` to `B`, both need to carefully consider what is happening. `A` might end up leaking data it does not want to leak. `B` might receive input it did not expect and take an action that harms the user. In particular, `B` should never trust `A`, as at some point cite118†URLs from `A` can come from untrusted sources.
L279: ## 3. Hosts (domains and IP addresses)
L280: 
L281: At a high level, a cite71†host , cite147†valid host string , cite99†host parser , and cite148†host serializer relate as follows:
L282: 
L283:   * The cite99†host parser takes an arbitrary cite106†scalar value string†infra.spec.whatwg.org and returns either failure or a cite71†host .
L284: 
L285:   * A cite71†host can be seen as the in-memory representation.
L286:   * A cite147†valid host string defines what input would not trigger a cite66†validation error or failure when given to the cite99†host parser . I.e., input that would be considered conforming or valid.
L287: 
L288:   * The cite148†host serializer takes a cite71†host and returns an cite70†ASCII string†infra.spec.whatwg.org . (If that string is then cite99†parsed , the result will cite149†equal the cite71†host that was cite148†serialized .)

Recommended metadata retrieval design for the implementation plan:

### Request flow

1. `POST /api/metadata` accepts only JSON `{ url }`, same-origin requests, and a small body. Check the normalized URL for an existing active/archived bookmark before any outbound request; duplicates should route directly to that bookmark without fetching.
2. Parse with the WHATWG `URL` implementation, then permit only `http:` and `https:`.
3. Reject credentials, empty/single-label hosts, `localhost`, `.localhost`, `.local`, IANA special-use names, fragments for retrieval, and non-default ports. A bookmark using another HTTP(S) port may still be saved manually, but automatic retrieval should fail safely.
4. Resolve all A/AAAA results using the OS resolver (`dns.lookup(host, {all:true})`), because it matches what Node networking uses. Reject the request if any answer is not globally routable.
5. Select one validated address and pin the actual connection to it through an explicit `undici` `Client`/dispatcher custom `connect.lookup`. Keep the original hostname in the URL so HTTP `Host`, TLS SNI, and certificate verification still use it. Use a disposable per-hop client and close it afterward; do not use an environment proxy.
6. Set `redirect: "manual"`. For each redirect, resolve `Location` against the current URL and repeat the complete validation, DNS resolution, and IP pinning. Allow at most 3 redirects and reject HTTPS→HTTP downgrade.
7. Apply exactly the same guarded fetch path to icon and preview-image URLs, including redirects. HTML-controlled `<base>` URLs never bypass validation.

This avoids the classic “validate one DNS lookup, connect using another” rebinding gap. Rejecting mixed public/private answers is intentionally conservative. A network egress rule denying private/link-local/cloud-metadata ranges should be added as defense in depth.

### Address policy

Maintain a checked-in deny-CIDR table derived from the IANA IPv4/IPv6 special-purpose registries; do not rely only on a library’s notion of “private.” Deny loopback, private/ULA, link-local, multicast, unspecified, documentation/benchmark ranges, carrier-grade NAT, IPv4-mapped IPv6, and transition/translation ranges such as NAT64/6to4. Canonicalize alternate IPv4 notations through the WHATWG parser before classification.

Also deny special hostnames before DNS resolution. This catches obvious cases early; resolved-address validation remains authoritative.

### Resource limits

Suggested v1 limits:

| Resource | Limit |
|---|---|
| DNS | 1 s |
| TCP/TLS connect | 1.5 s |
| Response headers | 2.5 s |
| Idle between body chunks | 1 s |
| Entire metadata operation | 5 s |
| Redirects | 3 |
| HTML decoded body | 1 MiB |
| Preview download | 5 MiB |
| Icon download | 1 MiB |
| Header bytes | 32 KiB |
| Preview decoded pixels | 20 MP; max side 4096 |
| Icon decoded pixels | 1 MP |
| Outbound concurrency | 4 globally, 2 asset downloads per metadata call |
| Retries | none |

Reject early when `Content-Length` exceeds the cap, but always count streamed decoded bytes too because length may be absent, false, or describe compressed content. Abort and destroy the response when a limit is crossed. Use the explicit Undici connect/header/body timeouts plus an overall abort signal.

Accept only `text/html` and `application/xhtml+xml` for the page. Parse XHTML in inert HTML mode—never an XML parser with external entities. No browser automation, scripts, styles, or page subresources should execute.

### Extraction

Decode using the declared/BOM/meta-sniffed HTML encoding, then parse with an inert parser such as Cheerio/parse5.

Recommended precedence:

- Title: `og:title` → `twitter:title` → `<title>`
- Description: `og:description` → `<meta name="description">` → `twitter:description`
- Preview: `og:image:secure_url` → `og:image` → `twitter:image`
- Icon: `<link rel="icon">` / `shortcut icon`, preferring useful declared sizes → `apple-touch-icon` → `/favicon.ico`

Resolve relative asset URLs against the valid first `<base href>` or final page URL, then put them through the guarded fetcher. Normalize whitespace/control characters and bound returned text (for example, title 300 characters, description 2,000). Treat absent or bad fields independently so title/description can succeed when images fail.

### Image handling and reliable caching

Never hotlink the remote icon or preview in the UI. It leaks the user’s viewing activity, can later break, and allows mutable third-party content.

For v1, store processed image bytes in SQLite:

```text
Asset(id_sha256 PK, kind, mime, bytes BLOB, width, height, created_at)
Bookmark(icon_asset_id FK nullable, preview_asset_id FK nullable)
```

- Require both an allowed response `Content-Type` and a matching binary signature.
- Accept raster JPEG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, GIF, and ICO; reject SVG and unknown formats.
- Decode only the first frame/page with Sharp, with a strict `limitInputPixels`.
- Re-encode preview to static WebP, max 1200×630; icon to static PNG, max 128×128. Sharp removes metadata by default.
- Hash the processed bytes with SHA-256 and deduplicate by hash.
- Commit bookmark references and asset rows in one SQLite transaction.
- Retrieval previews may create unreferenced staged assets; garbage-collect only unreferenced rows older than 24 hours.
- Serve through `/api/assets/:hash` with the stored MIME type, `Content-Length`, strong `ETag`, `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`, and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`.

SQLite BLOBs are preferable for this single-user v1 because the bookmark/asset relationship is crash-atomic. A content-addressed filesystem using temp-file + atomic rename is the later alternative if database growth becomes material; external object storage is unnecessary now.

### Failure behavior

Return typed, user-safe outcomes such as `invalid_url`, `blocked_destination`, `timeout`, `too_large`, `unsupported_content`, and `unreachable`; never expose resolved internal addresses or raw network errors. Any retrieval failure leaves URL/manual title entry usable. Asset failures do not discard successful text metadata.

Do not forward cookies, authorization, inbound headers, referrer, or client IP. Send a fixed user agent and narrow `Accept` headers. Keep TLS verification enabled. Add same-origin/Origin validation and no permissive CORS so another website cannot use the endpoint as a fetch oracle.

### Test strategy

- Table-driven URL tests: every scheme, credentials, alternate numeric IPv4 forms, percent encoding, IPv6 and IPv4-mapped IPv6, trailing dots, IDNs, special-use domains, ports, and overlong URLs.
- Resolver tests: public-only, private-only, mixed public/private, A-only, AAAA-only, no answer, and special IANA ranges.
- Rebinding test: fake resolver returns public during validation and private on a hypothetical second lookup; assert the connector uses the pinned public address and never performs that second lookup. Assert original Host/SNI remain intact.
- Redirect tests: relative and scheme-relative redirects, loops, excessive chains, redirect to `169.254.169.254`, private IPv6, credential-bearing URLs, forbidden ports, and HTTPS downgrade.
- Limit tests: absent/lying `Content-Length`, chunked overflow, gzip bomb, slow DNS/connect/headers/body, large headers, cancellation, and resource cleanup.
- Parser fixtures: extraction precedence, mixed casing, malformed HTML, duplicate tags, entities, legacy encodings, `<base>`, missing fields, and long/control-character text.
- Image tests: MIME/signature mismatch, SVG rejection, malformed images, decompression/pixel bombs, animations reduced to first frame, metadata stripped, dimensions capped.
- Persistence tests: hash deduplication, atomic bookmark+asset commit/rollback, staged-asset GC, shared-asset deletion safety, restart durability, and immutable asset responses.
- Run unit tests with injected resolver/transport/clock; integration tests use controlled HTTP/DNS fixtures and a test-only network policy, never weakening the production guard.

### Alternatives rejected

- Browser-side fetching: fails on CORS and exposes the user directly to remote sites.
- Plain `fetch(url)` after a DNS check: vulnerable to rebinding because the actual connection resolves again.
- Automatic redirects: lets redirect targets bypass validation.
- Remote image URLs stored directly: unreliable and privacy-leaking.
- Headless Chromium: excessive attack surface and resource cost for metadata available in HTML.
- SVG caching/rasterization in v1: adds active-content and parser risk with little user value.

Primary/current references:

- OWASP SSRF guidance: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html
- WHATWG URL parser/security model: https://url.spec.whatwg.org/
- IANA IPv4 registry: https://www.iana.org/assignments/iana-ipv4-special-registry/
- IANA IPv6 registry: https://www.iana.org/assignments/iana-ipv6-special-registry/
- IANA special-use domains: https://www.iana.org/assignments/special-use-domain-names/
- Node DNS behavior: https://nodejs.org/api/dns.html
- Undici custom DNS lookup/client timeouts: https://github.com/nodejs/undici/blob/main/docs/docs/api/Client.md
- Undici manual redirects/abort support: https://github.com/nodejs/undici/blob/main/docs/docs/api/Fetch.md
- HTML metadata semantics: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/semantics.html
- Open Graph fields: https://ogp.me/
- Binary signature detection caveats: https://github.com/sindresorhus/file-type
- Sharp input controls: https://sharp.pixelplumbing.com/api-constructor/
- Sharp output/metadata behavior: https://sharp.pixelplumbing.com/api-output/
- SQLite transaction guarantees: https://www.sqlite.org/transactional.html
